<!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all t]] == About Kujūku Ōji == {{Main|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}
'''Kujūku Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Kujūku Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Kujūku Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Kujūku Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kujūku Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] [[:en:Kumano Nachi Taisha|Kujūku Ōji]]
== About Kujūku Ōji == {{Main|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}
'''Kujūku Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Kujūku Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Kujūku Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Kujūku Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kujūku Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] [[:en:Kumano Nachi Taisha|Kujūku Ōji]]
== About Kujūku Ōji == {{Main|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}
'''Kujūku Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Kujūku Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Kujūku Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Kujūku Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kujūku Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Kujūku Ōji == {{Main|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}
'''Kujūku Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Kujūku Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Kujūku Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Kujūku Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kujūku Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

== About Kujūku Ōji == {{Main|Kujūku Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}
'''Kujūku Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Kujūku Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Kujūku Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Kujūku Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kujūku Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = [[File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg|200px]] | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|アマテラス|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}, [[:en:Izanami|Izanami]], and five others | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

''' ('''{{ill|List of Ninety-Nine Ōji (Hidaka Town)|ja|九十九王子 (日高町)|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/List of Ninety-Nine Ōji (Hidaka Town)|lt=Takaie Ōji|error=九十九王子 (日高町)|oji=王子|qq=}}''') * '''Zendōji Ōji''' * '''Aitokusan Ōji''' * '''Kuama Ōji''' * '''Iwauchi Ōji''' * '''Shioya Ōji''' * '''{{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobo)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/2=ja|lt=Ueno Ōji|qq=}}''' - ('''{{ill|List of Ninety-Nine Ōji (Inami Town)|ja|九十九王子 (印南町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/3=九十九王子 (印南町)|lt=Tsu'i Ōji|error=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji (Inami Town)|oji=王子|qq=}}''')'''

Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370045]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515

Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370045]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602}} | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) | location = {{ill|Gobo|qid=Q847572}} }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370045]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=|1=Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360402}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602}} | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) | location = {{ill|Gobo|qid=Q847572}} }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=|1=Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360402}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602}} | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) | location = {{ill|Gobo|qid=Q847572}} }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370045]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=|1=Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360402}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602}} | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) | location = {{ill|Gobo|qid=Q847572}} }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370045]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=|1=Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360402}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602}} | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) | location = {{ill|Gobo|qid=Q847572}} }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370045]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of [[:en:Gobō, Wakayama|Gobo City]] {{reflist}}
== About Ninety-Nine Ōji == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
'''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines located along the [[:en:Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodō]], particularly along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi|qq=|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} routes, rapidly organized primarily between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners, who guided imperial and noble pilgrims traveling to Kumano. They served as places for prayers and protection.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] of 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|qq=|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}} declined significantly, and with the deterioration of the Kiiji route, many shrines fell into ruin. During the Muromachi period, Kumano pilgrimages lost their prominence, and despite attempts at restoration by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the Edo period, decline continued. Further loss of sites occurred due to the State Shinto system after the Meiji era, mergers of shrines, and urbanization.
This article specifically discusses the shrines among Ninety-Nine Ōji located in Gobō City.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Gobō City == Gobō City has six Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines. For {{ill|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|ja|上野王子 (御坊市)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)|qq=|1=Ueno Ōji Shrine (Gobo)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360402}}, see separate entry.
=== Zendōji Ōji === [[File:善童子王子.jpg|thumb|Zendōji Ōji]] '''Zendōji Ōji''' (善童子王子) is located southwest of Ōji Bridge over the Nishigawa River, with a small shrine.
Historical records include references in "Chūyūki" (1109), "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Ninety-Nine Ōjiki" (1473), and listed as a semi-fifth-level Ōji in "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref name="Heibon_1997_490">Heibonsha [1997: 490]</ref>. It was locally revered, merged into Yukawa Shrine in 1909, and designated as a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Tomiyasu 1347
=== Aitokusan Ōji === [[File:愛徳山王子跡.jpg|thumb|Aitokusan Ōji]] '''Aitokusan Ōji''' (愛徳山王子) is north of Hachiman-yama hill near Dōjōji Temple. The site, now a citrus orchard, has stone monuments. It merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908 and became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2167
=== Kuama Ōji === [[File:九海士王子.jpg|thumb|Kuama Ōji]] '''Kuama Ōji''' (九海士王子) is on the southern foothills of Hachiman-yama. Originally within a citrus orchard, a worship place was established nearby. Historical mentions include "Kumano Michi no Aida Guki" (1201), "Minkeiki" (1210), and "Kumano Engi" (1326)<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 231]</ref>. It was merged into Yoshida Hachiman Shrine in 1908. The original statue, thought to represent [[:en:Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], is now enshrined in Dōjōji as Princess Miyako. It became a city historic site in 1970.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Yoshida 2263-1
=== Iwauchi Ōji === [[File:岩内王子跡.jpeg|thumb|Iwauchi Ōji]] '''Iwauchi Ōji''' (岩内王子) is located on the left bank of the Hidaka River. Historical records date back to 1109, mentioning frequent damage from flooding. It was merged into Kumano Shrine (Gobō City) in 1908. A historical marker remains.
* Address: Gobō-shi, Iwauchi-aza Tabata 515
=== Shioya Ōji === {{infobox religious building | name = Shioya Ōji Shrine | image = File:塩屋王子 02.jpeg | address = Gobō-shi, Kitashioya 1145 | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602}} | Rank = Village Shrine | founded = Unknown | alternate names = Bijin Ōji | festival = October 19 (Procession, Lion Dance, Horse Racing) | location = {{ill|Gobo|qid=Q847572}} }} '''Shioya Ōji''' (塩屋王子) is on a hillside by the Ōji River, historically noted from 1109. Locally known as Bijin Ōji, theories suggest its name comes from the beautiful deity statue or scenic beauty. It is a Wakayama Prefectural Historic Site (1958) and part of the National Historic Site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji" (2018). Its shrine forest is a city-designated natural monument (1979).
=== Ueno Ōji === {{See|Ueno Ōji (Gobō City)}}
== Nearby Information == === Aitokusan Ōji Pilgrimage Path === Original sections of Kumano Kodō remain around Aitokusan Ōji and are part of the national historic site "Kumano Sankeimichi Kiiji"<ref name=oji />. <gallery> File:愛徳山王子跡北東参詣道.jpg|Aitokusan Ōji Northeast Path File:愛徳山王子竹林道.jpg|Bamboo Grove near Aitokusan Ōji </gallery>
